OpenConnect has no server of ours. Your data stays on this phone. Only what you switch on leaves it: your Garmin or Oura account, an AI provider if you add a key, and GitHub when you look for an update. With an AI on, activity names, splits and heart-rate halves go to it, but no GPS route or GPS points. Keys stay in the Android Keystore. The page What leaves your phone lists each one.
This is exactly what will be shared. It holds versions, what is switched on and what the last syncs did. It holds no keys, tokens, names, health values or routes. Paste it into a GitHub issue.

Your health data stays on this phone: there is no server of ours. Only what you switch on leaves it. If you add an AI key, a short summary of your numbers and activity names goes to that provider, never your route.

Everything is stored on this phone only. Import FIT, GPX or TCX files, or a whole ZIP archive: the exports of Garmin Connect and Strava work as they are. Or load demo data.

An open-source, offline-first alternative to Garmin Connect. Not affiliated with Garmin. Licence: AGPL-3.0, Bluetooth sync ported from Gadgetbridge.
Read your watch with a USB cable or a folder, follow your heart rate live over Bluetooth, or pull your data from your Garmin account.
Read the watch with a USB cable

Plug the watch into the phone with its cable (USB-C, or with an OTG adapter). OpenConnect then copies the activities and the all-day data stored on the watch: steps, heart rate, stress, Body Battery, sleep, HRV and SpO2. It goes straight from the watch to this phone, not through Garmin or the internet.
No Garmin watch found on the USB port. Check the cable and that the watch is switched on, then search again.

Shows your heart rate live from a Garmin watch that broadcasts it, or from a chest strap. On the watch, look for Sensors & accessories, Wrist heart rate, Broadcast heart rate (the names differ per model).

The watch can sync over Bluetooth with OpenConnect itself (above), be read with a cable or from a folder, or send live heart rate. Data from Garmin\'s servers comes in on the Garmin screen.
Read a folder with watch files

Your watch talks to the Garmin Connect app on your phone over Bluetooth, and Garmin keeps your data in its cloud. OpenConnect reads your own data from there with a personal key that only you can create. There is no server of ours in between.

Sync a Garmin watch over Bluetooth

Experimental. OpenConnect talks to the watch the way the Garmin Connect app does (the protocol Gadgetbridge worked out) and copies what is new: activities, steps, heart rate, stress, Body Battery, sleep and HRV. No cable, no Garmin account. The first time, Android pairs with the watch: put the watch in pairing mode (Settings, Connectivity, Phone, Pair phone) and confirm the code.

Looks for every kind of Garmin watch, golf watch and bike computer, by its name and by the model number it advertises. Heart rate straps, lights and scales are left out: there is nothing to sync from them. Models that are not on the list this sync was made for carry a note.
Not on the list this sync was ported from, and nothing was tried on this model. Syncing may fail; the Garmin account route is the safe one.
This model needs Garmin\'s newer sync protocol, which OpenConnect does not have, so some files may be missing. The Garmin account route is safer.
A watch paired with OpenConnect will in practice no longer sync with the Garmin Connect app. The files stay on the watch.
Pairing: confirm the code on the watch and the phone.
Could not connect to the watch: %1$s. If Garmin Connect is paired with this watch, use the Garmin account route instead.
The watch connected, but listed no files OpenConnect can read.
Pairing with the watch did not work. Put the watch in pairing mode (Settings, Connectivity, Phone, Pair phone) and try again.
Based on %1$d days with a reading.
Steady compared with the week before
Steps counted by your watch each day. Around 7,000 to 10,000 a day is linked with good health; the dashed line is 10,000.
Hours slept per night. Most adults do well on 7 to 9 hours; the dashed line is 8.
Your heart rate at rest. A lower number usually means better fitness; most adults sit between 50 and 80. A sudden rise can mean stress, illness or poor sleep.
Garmin\'s energy estimate, from 0 to 100. The line shows the highest value of each day: 75 or more means you charged well, under 50 means little recovery.
Heart rate variability overnight. It is personal: compare with your own normal, not with others. A drop of more than 10% below your average can mean you need rest.
Blood oxygen. 95 to 100% is normal; lower readings at altitude or from a loose watch are common, persistent values under 90% are worth asking a doctor about.
Breaths per minute. 12 to 20 at rest is normal; the value moves a little with fitness, illness and altitude.
Garmin\'s stress score from heart rate variability, 0 to 100: up to 25 is rest, 26 to 50 low, 51 to 75 medium, above 75 high.

A watch talks to one phone app at a time over Bluetooth. If Garmin Connect is your main app, keep it that way and let OpenConnect read the same data from your Garmin account (Garmin account screen) or from files. Use the Bluetooth sync here only when OpenConnect should be the watch\'s phone. Runs that arrive from more than one route are recognised and kept once.
Enter today\'s weight to start the trend.

OpenConnect compares your last seven nights with your own four-week baseline; this is not the HRV Status of Garmin.
Readiness is OpenConnect\'s own estimate. Sleep score, Body Battery and stress are the watch\'s numbers. No reading yet shows a dash.
OpenConnect\'s own 0 to 100 estimate from sleep, Body Battery, HRV, resting heart rate and stress, against your own normal. 70 or more means ready for a hard day, under 40 means take it easy.
The sleep score your watch gives each night, 0 to 100: 80 or more is good, 60 to 79 fair, below 60 poor. It weighs duration, deep and REM sleep and restlessness.
What you want to reach each week. The defaults follow common recommendations; set a goal to off with the minus button.
All goals are switched off. Turn them on in Settings.
This week %1$s points, your usual week %2$s
Clearly less than your recent norm. Fine for recovery; if it was not planned, an easy session gets you going again.
In line with the last four weeks. This is the range where fitness builds with the least risk.
More than usual. Fine for a short block, but plan an easier week after it.
A big jump over what your body is used to. This is the usual time for niggles and illness: back off a little.
OpenConnect\'s own estimate: minutes times an effort weight from your heart rate, this week against your 4-week average. Not Garmin\'s Training Load, not medical advice.

Save everything the app holds in one file: activities with their tracks, daily health, sleep, the readings of your watch, ring and bands, and your journal, shoes, training plan, race and goals. Restoring adds it back without removing or overwriting anything. Keys are never in the file. Export everything makes one ZIP with CSV, FIT and GPX files that other apps can read, with the backup inside.

Your Oura Ring gets its own tab here: readiness, sleep and activity scores, nights, heart rate, HRV, skin temperature and workouts. It is kept apart from your watch, so nothing is counted twice. Oura needs an active Oura Membership for this on a Gen3 ring or Oura Ring 4. Oura no longer gives personal tokens, so you make a small application of your own at Oura once.
Sign in at Oura\'s developer site, choose to create a new application, and enter %1$s as its redirect address. Oura then shows a client ID and a client secret.
Client secret (saved; leave empty to keep it)
This phone cannot keep a secret safely, so OpenConnect does not store an Oura login.

Your browser opens Oura\'s login. After you allow it, the browser comes back to OpenConnect and the last 30 days are synced. If it does not come back, copy the address the browser ends up on and paste it below.

Predicted race times from your best efforts, with Riegel\'s formula. Garmin\'s own Race Predictor is not available to apps, so this is OpenConnect\'s own estimate: the further a distance is from what you have run, the rougher it is.
Run at least 4 km with a track to get predictions.

Each planned run of the next 7 days becomes a structured workout (warm-up, intervals or tempo, cool-down) in a .fit file, copied over the USB cable to GARMIN/NewFiles on the watch. Intervals and tempo get a pace window from your predicted 10 km pace. Find them on the watch under Training. Not tried on a real watch yet.
Send the next 7 days to my watch (USB)

Make a workout here for the watch: a warm-up, a number of fast repeats with rest, and a cool-down. It is saved with the app, goes in the backup and is sent along with the button above. Nothing is sent anywhere else.
Distance per repeat (m, empty = by time)
Check the numbers: 1 to 50 repeats, 0.5 to 60 fast minutes, 0 to 30 rest seconds, 0 to 60 warm-up and cool-down minutes.
Check the pace: two numbers between 120 and 1200 seconds per kilometre, the fastest one first.
Check the distance: 100 to 50,000 metres per repeat.
%1$d workouts copied to the watch, %2$d were already there.
There are no planned runs in the next 7 days.
Set by you. The zones are percentages of this number.
The highest heart rate in your activities. If you know your own maximum, set it with the buttons.
There is no heart rate in your activities yet. Press + to set a maximum yourself.
No heart rate was recorded in the last 7 days.
Some activities have no heart-rate samples, only an average, so their time is a guess.
Not enough heart-rate time for a verdict yet: it needs half an hour in the zones within 7 days.
Mostly easy with some hard work: a good mix.
A lot of hard work (over 30 percent in zones 4 and 5). Make the easy days really easy.
Too much in the middle (over 40 percent in zone 3). Make easy runs easier and hard ones harder.
All easy (under 5 percent hard). Fine for building a base; add one hard session to get faster.
OpenConnect\'s own arithmetic on the heart rate your watch recorded, as a percentage of the maximum. Garmin\'s own zones can differ, and a wrist sensor can read too high. Not medical advice.
Zones from a maximum of %1$d bpm.
A guess: this activity has only an average heart rate, no samples.
No shoes added yet. Add a pair below and the activities of its sport count towards its kilometres.
Each activity goes on the newest pair of its sport that was in use that day; on an activity\'s own page you can put it on another pair. Kilometres come from your recorded activities.

Getting old: over 80 percent of its life.

Today is still open: any activity keeps your streak going.
Tap a day to see its activities.
A day counts when an activity starts on it (days are UTC days) and a week runs from Monday to Sunday. A streak is not broken until its day or week is over.
Editorial is the calm default: very large corners, hairline borders and serif titles. Sleek is the compact dashboard, Retro is the pixel look and Classic has small corners and serif titles.
Soft keeps the signals in the theme\'s family; clear gives each signal its own strong colour. The rings, tiles and charts follow this everywhere.
The orbs on the front page and the ring tab follow this thickness.
The wallpaper follows the hour: warm dawn light, the lake in daylight, a low evening sun and a moonlit night. The words stay readable throughout.
Choose the card under the battery and what else the front page shows.
Pick the card that sits under the battery.
No reading yet. Sync your watch or ring and this card fills in.
Your resting heart rate today. A lower rate usually means more recovery.
The day\'s average stress. Lower is calmer.
Last night\'s sleep, as your watch or ring recorded it.
Good day for a hard one
Your body is not fully recovered today.
You are carrying a lot of fatigue from the last weeks.
Readiness and fatigue both say take it easier.
Rested and ready: fatigue is low and readiness is high.
Needs at least two weeks of activities to work out your form.
Not enough training yet to judge your form.
Rested: fatigue is well below your fitness. A good moment for a race or a hard session.
Fitness and fatigue are in line. You can train as planned.
Some fatigue on board. That is normal and productive in a block of training; plan an easier day or week soon.
Far more fatigue than fitness. Back off for a few days before the next hard session.

Fitness is a slow average of your training load, fatigue a fast one. Form is the difference: above zero you are rested, below zero you carry fatigue. A hard week lowers form at once and raises fitness slowly; a rest week does the opposite.
OpenConnect\'s own estimate from minutes and heart rate, in its own units. It is not Garmin\'s Training Status, not TSS, and not medical advice.
How well your last six weeks of running fit each distance: your weekly kilometres and your longest run against what a typical plan asks.
%1$s asks about %3$s km a week and a longest run of %5$s km; you run %2$s km a week and your longest run was %4$s km.
Rules of thumb from common training plans, not a promise. A prediction for a distance you are far from is a long shot.
The middle value of your last runs with heart rate in the last eight weeks (%1$d runs).
Worked out from pace and heart rate (Daniels and Gilbert, Swain). Rough: a few ml either way, and heat, hills and tired legs are not counted. It is not Garmin\'s VO2 max and not medical advice.
Tap what applies. After a few weeks the Journal tab shows how those days go with your next night.
The night after a marked day against the nights after the other days. Red is a worse night.
Nothing to compare yet: a mark needs at least four nights with it and four without, with HRV, resting heart rate or sleep from your watch.
This shows what goes together, not what causes what, and a few weeks of notes say little. Not medical advice.
Resting heart rate or HRV has been off for %1$d days in a row.
Your resting heart rate and HRV have been off for days: take it easy.
Resting heart rate: %1$d beats above your normal.
Compared with your own last four weeks. It often goes with getting ill or too little rest. A rule of thumb from two numbers, not a diagnosis.
Hard and easy days alternate and there is rest in between: the pattern that is easiest on the body for the load.
The days look alike. An easy day or a rest day in the week would help.
Almost the same load every day. That tires you more than the same load spread with easy and hard days.
Foster\'s monotony (mean daily load divided by its spread) of the last seven days; strain is the week\'s load times it. OpenConnect\'s own load units, an estimate, not medical advice.
No sleep debt over the last %1$d nights.
A small sleep debt of %1$s h over the last %2$d nights.
A big sleep debt of %1$s h over the last %2$d nights: an early night pays back most.
Eight hours, a little more after a hard day and a quarter of the debt back each night (at most an hour). A suggestion, not medical advice.
No routes with a position yet. Activities with GPS show up here.
The brighter a square, the more different runs, rides or walks went through it.
Only your own routes on a plain grid: no map provider sees where you go.
%1$d times on this route, this one included.
Your best time on this route.
%1$s slower than your best here (%2$s on %3$s).
%1$s slower than your average on this route.
%1$s faster than your average on this route.
Easy runs and time on your feet. Keep the weekly distance steady and do not rush.
More distance, and the first harder runs: tempo, hills or intervals once a week.
The biggest weeks, with runs at race pace and your longest run.
Less distance, a little speed, and rest: arrive at the start with fresh legs.
Worked back from the race date. The kilometres are around what you run in a week now. A rule of thumb, not a coach and not medical advice.
No year with steps, sleep or activities yet.
Each month with data counts once; months without data stay out of the averages.
No year with activities or steps yet.
OpenConnect %1$d: %2$s km in %3$d activities, %4$s hours, %5$d active days, longest streak %6$d days.
Worked out on the phone from your activities and daily summaries. Nothing is sent anywhere until you press share.
Last 7 days: %1$d load, your usual week: %2$d (×%3$s)
Clearly less than your last four weeks: a rest week, or time to build up again step by step.
About what your body is used to: a good base to keep building from.
More than you are used to. Fine now and then, but follow it with an easy day.
A big jump in one week. That is the pattern that goes with overuse injuries: take it easy for a few days.
Your last 7 days against the average week of the four weeks before. OpenConnect\'s own load units, a rule of thumb, not medical advice.
Average %1$s h, give or take %2$d min (shortest %3$s h, longest %4$s h)
Your nights are about equally long, which lets the body plan for sleep.
Some nights are clearly longer or shorter than others. A fixed bedtime evens it out.
Your nights swing a lot in length. That feels like jet lag at home: a fixed bedtime and wake-up time help most.
The spread of the length of your last %1$d nights. Bedtimes are not stored, so this looks at length only. Not medical advice.
Last 7 days: %1$d bpm, your normal: %2$d bpm
A lower resting heart rate usually goes with good recovery and growing fitness.
Your resting heart rate sits where it normally does.
Higher than usual. Often tiredness, stress, heat, alcohol or the start of an illness: keep an eye on it.
Your last 7 days against the average of the 28 days before. A rule of thumb from one number, not medical advice.
The last 7 days against your step goal of %1$s (10,000 when your watch gives none). Days without steps are left out.
Opens Garmin\'s Connect IQ app on this phone, where you manage the watch faces and apps of your watch. Without that app the Play Store opens, so you can install it.
Connect IQ could not be opened: this phone has no Garmin app, no Play Store and no browser for it.
Recorded by the %1$s only. It is listed here, but it does not count in totals, training load, records or trophies, and it has no heart rate or route.

Oura\'s activity score, 0 to 100, from how much you moved, how often you trained and how well you rested in between. 70 or more is good, under 50 means a quiet stretch.

The lowest heart rate of the night as your ring measures it, usually a few beats under the resting heart rate of the day. Lower means better recovery; a rise over several nights can mean stress or illness.
How far your skin temperature was from your own normal during the night, in degrees Celsius. Within half a degree is usual; a rise of a degree or more over several nights can come with illness.

Only when you switch the source on or use the feature. Nothing else is ever sent, and there is no server of ours.
Garmin (personal.connectapi.garmin.com): your daily data and activities, when you use your own Garmin key. The key goes to this address and nowhere else.
Oura (cloud.ouraring.com, api.ouraring.com): signing in and your days, when you connect an Oura Ring.
Claude (api.anthropic.com): a short summary of your numbers and activity names, never your route, and what you type to the coach, when you add a Claude key.
Gemini (generativelanguage.googleapis.com): the same, when you add a Gemini key.
GitHub (api.github.com, github.com): the updater asks for the newest release and downloads it. It sends nothing about you, but GitHub sees your network address, like any website does.
